newsitem.title: FRANCE: France's Seguin wants euro plan to include jobs.
newsitem.headline: France's Seguin wants euro plan to include jobs.

text.p: Outgoing French National Assembly speaker Philippe Seguin, vowing not to give way on Europe to boost his political career, urged Europe's leaders on Sunday to plug a hole in plans for a single currency by pushing for jobs.

He said France must join the euro since it had approved it in a 1992 referendum, but the Maastricht Treaty must be implemented in an "intelligent" way that took account of Europe's deep-seated unemployment problem.
"That the treaty forgot about jobs is intolerable," Seguin, who campaigned against Maastricht in the 1992 poll, told TF1 television, a week ahead of a snap parliamentary election.
"The Europe we are in the process of building has deliberately ignored the problem of employment," he said.
Calling for Europe to dominate the last week of campaigning, Seguin said that despite his previous opposition there was no point in discussing now whether to put Maastricht into effect.
"The issue is not whether we introduce the euro, but how we do it, with whom and to what purpose," he said.
Seguin has toned down his anti-Maastricht rhetoric since emerging as the voters' favourite to replace fellow conservative Alain Juppe as prime minister, should there be a reshuffle.
Some French newspapers have speculated about a reshuffle on the orders of President Jacques Chirac even if Juppe's centre-right coalition holds power, as predicted in the polls.
But Seguin, a Gaullist politician often seen at odds with Juppe's style, said he would not renounce his ideas on Europe simply in order to occupy the prime minister's seat.
"As far as I am concerned, filling a post just for the pleasure of doing so and paying the price of sacrificing my own ideas is not my kind of thing," he said.
The last opinion polls published before a ban came into force on Sunday predicted Juppe's Gaullists and their centrist allies staying in government but with a reduced majority.
The first round of the two-stage election is on May 25 followed by a run-off ballot on June 1. ((-- Paris newsroom +331 4221 5452))
